title: From Manual Task to Measurable Automation in Seven Days
content:
Choose one task you performed twice this week: rename incoming files, prepare a status report, or copy approved records into a second system. Seven days is enough to build a small automation experiment. It is not a promise that a complex process will be production-ready by Friday.

The experiment should end with a decision supported by your own observations: keep the automation, narrow it, revise it, or stop. Avoid starting with a platform purchase. Start with a repeatable task, an output someone can check, and a safe way to return to the manual method.

Day one: observe the manual task

Perform one ordinary instance and record inputs, steps, exceptions, and output. Measure your actual effort rather than guessing from memory. Include time spent locating information, correcting mistakes, and confirming completion. Record waiting separately from hands-on work so the improvement target is clear.

Google's SRE discussion of toil distinguishes repetitive operational work from engineering that creates lasting improvement. Use that distinction to select a candidate, without assuming all manual judgment should disappear. A rare sensitive approval may need human attention even when data preparation can be automated.

Day two: write an input and output contract

Specify required fields, accepted file types, allowed destinations, and conditions that cause a stop. Choose one narrow task rather than “automate administration.” For a weekly report, identify the exact source records, reporting period, and review owner. Decide what missing information looks like.

Define an acceptance check before building. “Produces a file” is insufficient if the file can contain duplicate rows. Better checks include expected identifiers, permitted categories, totals reconciled against source records, and explicit handling of empty inputs. Use synthetic or non-sensitive samples while designing.

If the input is CSV, parse it with a real parser. Python's csv documentation explains dialect differences, quoting, and reader behavior. Splitting every line at commas can corrupt fields containing commas or line breaks. Also document encoding and how dates and identifiers should be interpreted.

Days three and four: build a dry-run path

Separate reading, transforming, validating, and writing. First produce a proposed result in an isolated location. Show what would change, which inputs were skipped, and why. Keep the original inputs intact. A dry run should not secretly trigger the same external actions as the live path.

Add a run identifier and enough information to connect each output to its source. Avoid logging secrets or unnecessary personal information. If the task sends messages or changes records, require a reviewable proposal until the user has authorized the operational scope.

Check exception cases before adding a schedule. Use an empty file, a missing required field, a duplicate identifier, and an unavailable destination. Decide whether each case should fail the whole run or produce a partial result clearly marked for review. Silent omission is rarely a useful default.

Day five: rehearse repetition and overlap

Run the same sample twice and inspect whether it duplicates work. A scheduler may retry after a timeout, and an operator may click twice. Give the task a stable identity or checkpoint so it can distinguish new work from already completed work.

If using GitHub Actions, its concurrency documentation explains grouping runs so they do not overlap and describes cancellation behavior. A concurrency setting is only one control; it does not automatically make an external write idempotent. Reconcile the destination state before retrying a possibly completed action.

Keep the schedule slower than your ability to inspect early results. A daily task that fails silently for a month creates a larger cleanup than a manual task performed carefully. Name the person who receives a meaningful failure alert and what action that person can take.

Day six: compare equivalent work

Compare the automated and manual paths on the same kind of input. Record hands-on effort, review effort, corrections, and failures separately. Include maintenance required by changed source formats. Do not claim a saving by excluding the human review the automation still needs.

Retain a small result log with input identity, proposed output, validation status, and reviewer decision. An unexpected result should be explainable from that evidence. If it is not, improve traceability before widening the task.

Day seven: make a bounded decision

A hypothetical weekly inventory report

Hypothetical example: a small workshop prepares an inventory summary from two approved CSV exports. It proposes a script that validates item identifiers, flags conflicting quantities, and writes a draft report. The script does not reorder stock. A person reviews conflicts and approves the final report.

The experiment would compare preparation and review effort with the existing manual process. No times saved or error reductions are asserted here. If the exports lack stable identifiers, the next decision may be to improve source data before continuing automation.

Operating checklist

  • Is the task narrow enough to describe with explicit inputs and outputs?
  • Does dry run avoid external side effects?
  • Are repeated runs and partial completion handled?
  • Do invalid inputs create visible, actionable failures?
  • Is review effort included in the comparison?
  • Can an owner disable the schedule and resume manual work?

A small, measured automation that handles its limits is useful. Expanding it should be a separate decision based on the evidence, not the automatic reward for reaching the end of the week.
excerpt: Turn one manual task into a seven-day automation experiment with a dry run, exception checks, repeated-run handling, and an honest comparison.
